objectives.text: Identify the guest group and preferences, and explain plans by distinguishing meals, number of nights and conditions.

sections.title: Start with the guest’s wishes
sections.body: Planning combines rooms, meals, local experiences and other resources to meet a particular group’s needs. It can include overnight stays, day visits or lunch events. Before listing facilities, establish the purpose of the trip, companions and preferred way to spend the stay. This helps define the value offered. Use inquiries and guest feedback to establish needs rather than assuming that everyone in a group wants the same thing.

sections.title: One night with two meals versus B&B
sections.body: A one-night, two-meal plan combines one overnight stay with dinner and breakfast. B&B means bed and breakfast: accommodation with breakfast. Dinner is not necessarily included in a breakfast-inclusive booking. Explain the meals separately when discussing the price; the phrase “meals included” alone does not tell the guest which meals are covered.

sections.title: Consecutive nights and benefits
sections.body: A consecutive-night stay means two or more successive nights at the same property. Some properties offer discounts or benefits, but these are not automatic. Check the minimum number of nights, eligible dates and other terms of the plan currently on sale. Checking the number of meals separately from the number of nights helps avoid missing a meal during the stay.

sections.title: Walk-ins and deposits
sections.body: A walk-in arrives and requests service without a prior reservation. Do not treat the request as an existing booking; check current availability and acceptance conditions. A deposit is money held for purposes such as guaranteeing use of services. Distinguish it from the room price itself and follow the accounting procedure so that you can explain what the amount is for.

sections.title: The scope of all-inclusive plans
sections.body: All-inclusive is a way of bundling accommodation with specified services, such as food, drinks or activities. The name does not mean that every property or product includes exactly the same things. Check included services, available times and chargeable extras in the actual plan description. Explain specifically what is included and what costs extra.

sections.title: Travel style and repeat visits are different classifications
sections.body: FIT refers to an independent traveler who plans and undertakes their own trip rather than relying solely on a group package. A repeat guest returns to a property they have used before. Travel arrangements and past use of a property are different classifications: an independent traveler can also be a repeat guest. Use these terms to explore information needs, not to stereotype guests.

objectives.text: Distinguish rooms sold, rooms available and room revenue; calculate the three indicators with correct percentage conversion.

sections.title: Use the same scope and period
sections.body: Keep rooms sold, available rooms and room revenue distinct in the records. For one day’s performance, use the same date and room scope for numerator and denominator. Examples in this course assume every room is available and there are no additional issues such as cancellations, complimentary rooms or tax treatment. Do not add restaurant or shop revenue to room revenue. Figures from different conditions cannot be compared by looking at the numbers alone.

sections.title: OCC shows room utilization
sections.body: OCC is the room occupancy rate. In the example, calculate rooms sold ÷ rooms available × 100 to obtain a percentage. If 30 of 40 rooms are sold, 30 ÷ 40 × 100 = 75%. State whether the numbers are booking forecasts or actual sales after the stay. The reference explains the calculation using reserved rooms and total rooms; keep forecasts and actual performance separate.

sections.title: ADR divides by rooms sold
sections.body: ADR represents average room revenue per room sold. Calculate room revenue ÷ rooms sold in these examples. Revenue of ¥360,000 from 30 rooms gives ¥12,000 per room. Including the ten unsold rooms in the denominator would measure something different. A high ADR alone does not prove that the property has maximized total sales or profit.

sections.title: RevPAR and percentage conversion
sections.body: RevPAR is room revenue per available room. Here, ¥360,000 ÷ 40 = ¥9,000 per room. With the same scope, it also equals ADR × OCC expressed as a decimal: ¥12,000 × 0.75 = ¥9,000. Multiplying by 75 instead of 0.75 produces a result 100 times too large. If using the percentage number, calculate ¥12,000 × 75 ÷ 100.

sections.title: Check units and rounding
sections.body: Show OCC as a percentage and ADR and RevPAR as yen per room in these examples. Retain precision during the calculation and round only the final result to the specified place. If no rooms are sold, ADR cannot be calculated by dividing room revenue by rooms sold because the denominator is zero. Keep the date, room counts, revenue and units so another person can reproduce the calculation.

sections.title: Do not decide from one indicator
sections.body: Demand changes between busy and quiet periods, and occupancy tends to change too. Cutting prices only to fill rooms reduces the room rate and affects revenue. A high rate can also result in lower total room revenue if the number of rooms sold falls greatly. Explain performance using OCC, ADR and RevPAR together, considering both price and volume.

sections.title: Basic terms for demand and pricing
sections.body: Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to bookings, availability or similar conditions. Revenue management considers demand and selling methods in light of the fact that an unsold room-night today cannot be carried forward as tomorrow’s stock. Raising or lowering prices is not the goal in itself. Examine both occupancy and rate to understand outcomes under the stated conditions.

choices: Calculate by dividing by zero.

questions.explanation: Division by zero is not possible. Record why the value cannot be calculated instead of inventing an actual figure.

choices: Conclude profit increased from ADR alone.
Check OCC and RevPAR over the same period and scope.
Delete the room-sales records.
Add percentages as though they were yen.
questions.explanation: Assess both rate and volume. Room-revenue indicators do not by themselves measure profit after expenses.

choices: Dynamic pricing / revenue management

questions.explanation: Dynamic pricing concerns price adjustment; revenue management considers demand and the room-selling opportunity.

objectives.text: Check facility information, the booking path and updates from the perspective of guests seeking the information they need.

sections.title: Publicity audiences and purposes
sections.body: Publicity communicates the property’s or company’s activities to build understanding and trust. Audiences include travelers, business partners, employees, local residents and shareholders. For attracting guests, explain specifically how the property’s strengths differ from others. Alongside the property’s own communications, reviews from past guests can introduce the property to new people.

sections.title: Can guests reach the information they need?
sections.body: Make entrances to rates, rooms, access and reservations easy to find. A beautiful website can still obstruct bookings if guests cannot locate availability. Act as a real visitor, look for information and review the layout and wording of navigation.

sections.title: Reduce uncertainty before booking
sections.body: Organize room and property facilities, rates, maps and transport access. Photos and video help guests imagine using the rooms, shared spaces and surrounding area. When facilities or prices change, update both the text and image descriptions. The Level 2 reference also includes nearby sightseeing information, supporting guidance about the whole local stay.

sections.title: Online reservations and direct booking
sections.body: A property’s own reservation function lets guests request dates that suit their schedule. Booking directly with the property without an agency or OTA is direct booking. It can reduce intermediary commission, but clear terms and confirmation screens remain important. Identify the booking route and check for contradictory information about the same room across channels.

sections.title: Search visibility and useful content
sections.body: SEO improves the chance that people searching for relevant information will find the site. Use language matching the property’s characteristics and answer visitors’ questions. A list of keywords does not remedy missing information about rates or equipment. Check both discoverability and the usefulness of information after the visitor arrives.

sections.title: Keep updating and improving
sections.body: Gather guest feedback to find unclear information and dissatisfaction with rooms or services. Regularly check rates, campaigns and facilities, and remove or correct expired information. Recording the responsible person, date and changes also helps handovers. The purpose is not merely to perform updates, but to keep correct information available to guests.

objectives.text: Organize a post’s purpose, audience and local cooperation, then use responses to improve communication.

sections.title: Choose whom to address and what to communicate
sections.body: SNS can introduce a property and develop relationships with guests. Select useful topics such as room or food photos, local attractions, events and offers. Before posting, state whose question the content answers. Rather than merely arranging similar photos, explain the situation in which guests could use or enjoy the service.

sections.title: Plan sustainable posting
sections.body: Consistency matters, but every property does not need the same posting frequency. The reference gives examples from several times weekly to daily; choose a schedule suited to the audience and operating capacity. Assign staff and content, and do not make an old event look current. Balance regular activity with accuracy.

sections.title: Respond to questions and comments
sections.body: Replies are opportunities to continue relationships. Use information verified by the property and avoid leaving questions unanswered. Reacting to guest posts can also build interaction, but align responses with the property’s policy. Reading what people say is part of the role, alongside sending messages.

sections.title: Communicate local attractions together
sections.body: Cooperation with tourism associations and local businesses can explain attractions beyond the accommodation itself. Methods include introducing one another’s accounts or publicizing joint campaigns. Confirm dates and conditions with partners so separate posts do not contradict one another. Giving people more reasons to visit the area can also support property use.

sections.title: Use guest experiences appropriately
sections.body: Guest photos and reviews offer experience-based information different from the property’s own presentation. Shared hashtags and campaigns help locate such posts. However, public visibility does not mean the property is free to reuse photographs. Check permission and operating policy before using them. This is a reuse check, not a claim that public posts may be used without conditions.

sections.title: Use results to change the next post
sections.body: Use analytics to monitor responses and follower activity over time. Do more than collect popular photos: consider which topics and timing reached the intended audience. Form a hypothesis, change content or timing and compare later responses. Record changes as evidence for future communication decisions.

terms.meaning: Publishing text or images on SNS or another platform.

objectives.text: Distinguish PMS, booking engines and OTA roles, and assess sales proposals based on guest groups and added value.

sections.title: PMS combines property operations information
sections.body: PMS stands for Property Management System: software managing reservations, front-desk operations, room status, guest information and accounting. Departments need different information, but contradictory records obstruct handovers. Assess functions against the property’s scale and work. The label PMS does not mean every product offers identical functions.

sections.title: Distinguish booking engines from PMS
sections.body: A booking engine accepts guest reservations on the property’s own website. PMS manages internal operations, while the engine principally provides the booking entrance. This distinction helps separate a guest’s inability to submit a reservation from conflicting internal room records. Confirm actual integrations and their update timing.

sections.title: OTA and direct booking roles
sections.body: An OTA is an online travel agency handling travel products and accommodation. Its contracting and commission route differs from direct booking. Direct bookings may reduce intermediary fees; benefits or pricing terms can be selling points. However, describe best-rate guarantees and benefits only after checking what the property actually offers.

sections.title: Do not treat commission rates as fixed rules
sections.body: OTA commission is not necessarily identical across channels or amounts sold. The reference mentions approximately 8–15% of sales, treated here as an example in the 2024 text. Do not apply it to an estimate without checking the current contract and calculation basis. Exercises must state the assumed rate and amount to which it applies.

sections.title: Inbound, FIT and VIP are different classifications
sections.body: Inbound refers to tourism or business involving travelers arriving from overseas. FIT describes how a trip is arranged; VIP is a category for guests requiring special treatment at the property. These are different dimensions: an overseas independent traveler may also be a property VIP. Share the actual information and service needed, not just the label.

sections.title: Pair upselling with added value
sections.body: Upselling encourages guests to choose a higher-level product or service. When suggesting an upgraded room, explain how its space or equipment serves the guest’s purpose. Do not confirm a change without stating the surcharge or pressure guests into something unsuitable. Let the guest decide and communicate the chosen outcome to relevant departments.

A mechanism accepting bookings through a property’s website.
An online travel agency handling travel products and accommodation bookings.

objectives.text: Compare prices and rooms sold using demand and performance, without confusing room revenue with profit.

sections.title: An unsold room-night cannot be carried forward
sections.body: A room-night not sold today cannot be added to tomorrow’s stock. Revenue management considers this characteristic when assessing rates and rooms offered in light of seasonal demand and sales forecasts. Avoid treating rushed sales on busy days and empty rooms on quiet days with one identical approach; check booking movements and past results.

sections.title: Read history alongside the market
sections.body: Level 2 uses past sales and market trends to forecast peak demand. The same period last year is one input, but consider differences in this year’s events and booking pace. A forecast is not an established fact. Record its basis, compare it with later performance and revise it.

sections.title: Understand the purpose of changing prices
sections.body: Dynamic pricing adjusts prices according to demand, reservations or similar conditions. Raising or lowering a price is not inherently good or bad. Anticipate effects on room volume and rates, and align decisions with approval procedures and sales terms. Do not confuse existing booking conditions with newly offered prices.

sections.title: Yield management includes volume
sections.body: Yield management considers not only price but how many rooms to offer under particular conditions. Heavy discounts to increase occupancy lower the rate, while too little discounting can leave rooms unsold. Use historical demand and sales movements to assess price and volume combinations, then compare concrete figures rather than assuming one measure is best.

sections.title: Compare alternatives with the same availability
sections.body: For a practice day with all 50 rooms available, option A sells 30 rooms at ¥15,000: room revenue ¥450,000, OCC 60%, ADR ¥15,000 and RevPAR ¥9,000. Option B sells 40 at ¥12,000: revenue ¥480,000, OCC 80%, ADR ¥12,000 and RevPAR ¥9,600. A has the higher rate, but under these assumed volumes B has higher room revenue and RevPAR.

sections.title: Separate higher revenue from higher profit
sections.body: Higher room revenue alone does not prove higher profit. Profit assessment also needs information such as additional expenses, which OCC, ADR and RevPAR alone do not provide. In option B, the stated assumptions support higher room revenue, but not a profit conclusion without costs. Report what can be established and what needs further checking separately.

sections.title: Check transport-inclusive products before selling
sections.body: The Level 2 reference warns about travel-business registration when selling accommodation bundled with transport to the property. Combining a room with a local experience is not the same as arranging or selling transport. Before implementation, present the product and contracting/arranging parties to the responsible manager and check current rules and the property’s authority. This lesson alone does not determine whether registration is required.

questions.prompt: Which is appropriate demand forecasting?
choices: Compare historical data with current booking and market movements.
Assume this year must equal last year.
Never revise forecasts because they are facts.
Remove all information except price.
questions.explanation: Use history while checking current differences and revising the forecast.

questions.prompt: Which appropriately describes dynamic pricing?
choices: Always reduce rates every day.
Change existing bookings without explanation.
Check occupancy but never price.
Adjust prices with demand and booking conditions, considering volume effects.
questions.explanation: Consider demand, room volume and rates together rather than changing prices as an end in itself.

questions.prompt: All 50 rooms are available. A: 30 × ¥15,000; B: 40 × ¥12,000. Which is correct?
choices: A’s RevPAR is ¥15,000.
B’s room revenue is ¥480,000 and RevPAR is ¥9,600.
B’s ADR must exceed A’s.
A’s OCC is 30%.
questions.explanation: B revenue = 40 × ¥12,000 = ¥480,000. Divide by 50 available rooms for RevPAR ¥9,600.

questions.prompt: B has higher room revenue, but no costs are provided. What can be said?
choices: Profit must also be higher.
Costs are irrelevant.
Room revenue is higher under the assumptions; profit comparison needs more information.
The predicted sales volume is certain.
questions.explanation: Revenue comparison and profit comparison differ. Check costs and the forecast basis.

questions.prompt: A new product bundles accommodation and transport. What is appropriate?
choices: Start selling unconditionally from one reference sentence.
Identify arranging/contracting parties and check current rules with the responsible manager.
No check is needed if transport is written in small print.
An accommodation property can always sell every travel product.
questions.explanation: Applicability depends on product details and other conditions. This lesson does not settle operational permission.

illustration.caption: Keep available rooms constant when comparing combinations of rate and rooms sold.
illustration.alt: Comparison for 50 available rooms: A sells 30 at ¥15,000 for ¥450,000, OCC 60%, RevPAR ¥9,000; B sells 40 at ¥12,000 for ¥480,000, OCC 80%, RevPAR ¥9,600.

lessons.title: Forecast demand and assess room prices and sales volume

objectives.text: Distinguish market segmentation from target selection, and combine value, channels and improvement measures in one plan.

sections.title: Segmentation divides a market
sections.body: Segmentation groups guests with different needs according to criteria such as travel purpose or behavior. Business visitors on short stays may prioritize different information from people taking a slow sightseeing trip. Classification is a planning tool, not proof that everyone in a group wants the same thing. State the criteria, then establish each group’s needs.

sections.title: Targeting selects whom to focus on
sections.body: Targeting chooses which segment the property will prioritize. Consider whether it can meet the needs, use its strengths and expect returns. Dividing the market does not itself complete target selection. Explain the selection and share the same target understanding across rooms, meals, guidance and publicity.

sections.title: A brand consistently communicates distinctive value
sections.body: Branding consistently explains what the property values and the stay it offers. Service and plan explanations shape the impression alongside photographs. Greater understanding and awareness may support repeat use and choice based on more than price. Select characteristics that actual service can demonstrate rather than merely repeating the word luxury.

sections.title: The role of a press release
sections.body: A press release formally informs the media about new products, events, company activities or performance. Its purpose and audience may differ from everyday SNS posts. Organize what will be communicated, when and to whom, and clearly provide verified facts and a contact point. Share the announcement internally so inquiry responses remain consistent.

sections.title: Connect reviews with experience and improvement
sections.body: Word of mouth grows from guests sharing experiences through OTA, review sites and SNS. It reflects actual impressions rather than only what the property wants to say. Read beyond ratings to identify mentioned equipment or service, and use the findings to improve both operations and explanations. Reduce gaps between actual experience and publicity, recognizing the influence of reviews on reputation and bookings.

sections.title: Assess the basis and conditions of plan counts
sections.body: The Level 2 reference gives a range of 6–15 plans for a property website. That number alone is not a universal optimum. Treat it as a statement from that reference and check whether guests can distinguish similar offers, choose easily and whether the property can operate them. Use property data and sales policy when deciding the actual number.

sections.title: Align one plan across multiple channels
sections.body: Once target guests and value are defined, keep rates, dates and conditions consistent across the website, SNS and media announcements. Length can differ by channel, but the service offered must not change in the telling. Gather inquiries and reactions to check whether the intended audience was reached and offers were easy to choose. Share improvements across planning, publicity and operations.

terms.meaning: Dividing a market or guest base by specified criteria.
Choosing priority audiences from the segments.
Building recognition through consistent communication of distinctive value.
A formal announcement prepared for the media.
How widely a property or its characteristics are known.
A means or place used to communicate information.

example.situation: A weekday plan targets people who want leisurely local walks, but staff use inconsistent promotional descriptions.
steps: Segment by travel purpose and choose the priority audience.
Share the available stay value and reasons for the selection.
Align dates, rates and inclusions across the site, SNS and announcements.
Gather inquiries and post-stay feedback and improve with operations staff.

practice.prompt: Give two segmentation criteria, choose one guest group, and explain the property’s value and suitable communication channels.
expectedPoints: Distinguish dividing the market from selecting a target.
Choose value the property can actually deliver.
Keep sales conditions consistent across channels.
Use reviews and inquiries as improvement evidence.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes dividing guest groups by trip purpose and then choosing a priority audience?
choices: Divide = targeting / choose = ADR
Divide = PMS / choose = SEO
Divide = segmentation / choose = targeting
Divide = word of mouth / choose = deposit
questions.explanation: Segmentation divides a market; targeting selects a focus from those segments.

questions.prompt: Which is appropriate branding?
choices: Communicate deliverable, distinctive property value through consistent explanations and service.
Create different conditions for every channel.
Only repeat the word luxury.
Assume awareness never relates to repeat use.
questions.explanation: Align communication with actual experience to explain why guests should choose the property.

questions.prompt: Which formally presents a new local partnership product to the media?
choices: Room key
Deposit receipt
Only an occupancy table
Press release
questions.explanation: A press release is a formal announcement for media use.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate approach to guest reviews?
choices: Read ratings but not comments.
Organize mentions of facilities and service to improve operations and explanations.
Do not collect them because they are unrelated to publicity.
Continue inaccurate promotion if some reviews are good.
questions.explanation: Use evaluation of actual experiences to align service and communication.

questions.prompt: The reference mentions 6–15 website plans. How should this be handled?
choices: As a legal maximum for every property.
Say 16 plans is necessarily illegal.
Separate the reference statement from a universal optimum and check ease of choice and property data.
Guarantee sales growth from the count alone.
questions.explanation: Do not turn a source-specific recommendation into an obligation or universally optimal number.

questions.prompt: What is most important when communicating the same plan through several channels?
choices: Align rates, dates and conditions, and share feedback with operations.
Add unapproved extra benefits only on SNS.
Make the wording exactly the same character by character.
Withhold inquiries from planners.
questions.explanation: Wording can suit the channel, but sales conditions and promised value must be consistent.

illustration.caption: Distinguish dividing the market from choosing a focus within it.
illustration.alt: Diagram selecting one of three travel-purpose segments, then consistently communicating its matched property value through website, SNS and media materials.

lessons.title: Choose target guests and align branding and publicity
